abstract: Adapting large language models (LLMs) for time series forecasting introduces unique challenges due to the mismatch between continuous time series tokens and the discrete word tokens LLMs are trained on. While LLMs have shown success on natural language tasks, aligning time series tokens with the semantic space of LLMs while preserving both accuracy and interpretability remains an open problem. Existing reprogramming and prompt-based approaches often generate word embeddings that are misaligned with or semantically irrelevant to the corresponding time series. For example, a segment with an increasing trend may be mapped to words like ”mirror” or ”keyboard”, which makes them hard to interpret. To bridge the gap, we propose MLTA-LLM, a Multi-Level Text Alignment framework for time series forecasting with LLMs. MLTA-LLM decomposes time series into trend, seasonal, and residual components, each of which is aligned with semantic anchor embeddings or text prototype embeddings. This component-specific alignment forces the LLM to process time series data through structured, interpretable representations. In addition, we integrate conformal prediction to provide statistically rigorous prediction intervals for uncertainty quantification. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show that MLTA-LLM not only improves forecasting accuracy over state-of-the-art baselines but also yields more interpretable representations and better-calibrated uncertainty estimates.

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have attracted great attention in both academic and industrial communities in recent years. Numerous survey studies have covered various aspects of LLMs, such as learning strategies, applications, alignment, explainability, and evaluation. However, little headway has been made in reviewing data-related aspects for LLMs, despite data being recognized as a key factor contributing to the emergence of the LLMs era. A wide range of data optimization algorithms and techniques are employed in LLMs’ training and application processes. These techniques often originate from diverse deep learning domains, with their theoretical inspirations and heuristic motivations appearing unrelated to each other. This study aims to develop a comprehensive framework for LLMs’ data optimization techniques to enhance data utilization and efficiency. We first discuss data challenges in LLMs’ training and inference. Second, we summarize data perception dimensions for evaluating LLMs’ data properties. These dimensions primarily include quality, difficulty, diversity, and redundancy, laying a foundation for subsequent optimization. Third, existing optimization techniques are reviewed and categorized into four groups: data selection, augmentation, reweighting, and others. Fourth, we analyze interconnections between these categories. Finally, we identify key challenges and future directions for LLMs’ data optimization compared with conventional deep learning approaches.

abstract: Transmission delays are inherent in silicon photonic integrated circuits (PICs) and have a significant impact on their dynamic behavior and system-level performance. However, conventional modeling and simulation approaches often overlook or inadequately account for these delays, limiting accuracy and efficiency in circuit-level analysis. This paper presents a delay-aware macromodeling methodology that explicitly extracts time delays from frequency-domain responses and incorporates them into a compact pole-residue representation. In contrast to traditional techniques such as complex vector fitting (CVF), which approximate delay effects indirectly and often require a large number of poles, resulting in increased model complexity, reduced simulation efficiency, and potential causality violations, the proposed method captures delays explicitly and compactly without compromising accuracy or physical consistency. To enable integration into circuit simulation workflows, we introduce an efficient Verilog-A implementation of the proposed model, along with practical strategies for representing time delays within standard electronic-photonic co-simulation environments. The proposed approach is validated using three categories of passive PIC structures: waveguides, feedforward multi-path circuits, and resonant (loop-based) circuits, demonstrating superior compactness, simulation speed, and accuracy compared to conventional modeling techniques. These results highlight the method’s potential for scalable and high-fidelity modeling of PICs in hybrid electronic-photonic circuit and system design.

abstract: High-Level Synthesis (HLS) design productivity is often constrained by manual, expert-driven pragma tuning and the difficulty of balancing performance optimization with strict hardware resource limits. While automated Design Space Exploration (DSE) has been extensively studied, many existing approaches rely on open-loop estimation models or substantial training data, which can lead to physically unrealizable designs under tight resource budgets. In this work, we propose Reflex-HLS , a training-free agentic framework that formulates HLS optimization as a closed-loop, feedback-driven process grounded in physical synthesis outcomes. Reflex-HLS integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) within a Planner–Actor–Critic architecture, where optimization decisions are iteratively refined based on hardware-in-the-loop feedback from the vendor toolchain, ensuring physical realizability throughout the optimization process. Experimental results on PolyBench and MachSuite benchmarks, validated through full Vivado synthesis and implementation, demonstrate that Reflex-HLS achieves speedups of up to 48.41 × (e.g., on jacobi-2d ) while strictly adhering to device resource constraints. Further evaluations across regular, irregular, and structured workloads show that the proposed framework generalizes beyond conventional compute kernels. Comparative studies against representative open-loop DSE methods, large foundation models operating without hardware feedback, and closed-loop heuristic search highlight the trade-offs among optimization paradigms, with Reflex-HLS producing more deployable and resource-efficient designs under tight resource budgets in the evaluated cases.

abstract: As advanced process nodes continue to scale, heterogeneous integration technologies such as 2.5D/3D packaging, chiplets, and high-bandwidth memory have been widely adopted. However, these advances introduce substantially higher power densities, more complex interconnection structures, and increasingly diverse material systems. The resulting localized hotspots raise reliability concerns such as electromigration, thermomechanical stress, and structural warpage, making layout-driven thermal simulation with balanced accuracy and efficiency essential for rapid design iterations. This paper proposes AceTherm, an automated thermal simulation framework driven by Graphic Data System (GDS) layout and Process Design Kit (PDK) process parameters, which integrates non-conformal finite element method with customized sparse-matrix solvers. By exploiting the layered structure of the chip architecture, the simulation domain is sampled and discretized with a non-conformal mesh and high-resolution material mapping, significantly reducing degrees of freedom (DOFs) while preserving accuracy. The mesh division and sampling resolution provide a two-level control for trading off accuracy and speed, and the convergence and error behavior are analyzed to characterize the discrete scheme of AceTherm. Exploiting the structural properties of the resulting coefficient matrix, AceTherm employs supernodal sparse Cholesky factorization to accelerate the solution process. Notably, the symbolic factorization can be reused across multiple thermal load scenarios when the mesh pattern remains unchanged. Numerical experiments show that the proposed method achieves a 104.6 × speedup over the conventional COMSOL solution and reaches up to 539.2 × in repeated or preset-parameter simulations, while maintaining the average temperature error below 1 K. The combination of high computational speed, layer-aware modeling, and sub-Kelvin accuracy positions AceTherm as a practical tool for thermal analysis and optimization in heterogeneous IC back-end design.

abstract: low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes are extensively utilized in triple-level cell (TLC) NAND flash memory due to their robust data error correction capability, with their performance dependent on the decoder’s iterative computation of the Log-Likelihood Ratio (LLR) messages transmitted by the NAND flash memory channel. However, implementing LDPC decoding algorithms in hardware necessitates the quantization of LLR messages due to limited hardware resources, which inevitably diminishes LLR accuracy and subsequently affects LDPC decoding performance. To mitigate this issue, we propose a classification-based graded LLR Quantization Scheme for 3D TLC NAND Flash, termed CGLLR. By employing the k-means clustering algorithm to categorize the quantized initial LLR messages from the channel, we apply distinct quantization factors to different categories of LLR values while preserving the relative magnitudes among the original LLR. This CGLLR strategy significantly enhances the resolution of LLR messages, thereby improving decoding performance. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed CGLLR scheme reduces the average number of decoding iterations by 26.3% compared to the standard algorithm.

abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have recently achieved major gains across many domains, increasing the need for hardware accelerators that can adapt to changing workloads. Because DNN layers have diverse characteristics, each may benefit from a different hardware architecture. FPGAs support this through runtime reconfiguration, but applying it to neural network accelerators remains limited. Reconfiguring the FPGA between every pair of layers would tailor hardware to each layer but incur prohibitive reconfiguration overhead. We address this by proposing a cluster-based approach that groups layers with similar computational requirements and assigns each group a shared hardware configuration. This reduces the number of reconfigurations while preserving efficient execution. However, selecting good clusters and configurations creates a large design space, especially for large networks: too few clusters merges dissimilar layers and hurts efficiency, while too many clusters increases reconfiguration overhead. To tackle this, we present a Design-Space Exploration (DSE) framework that co-optimizes clustering schemes and hardware configurations using genetic algorithms. Our method explores clustering schemes without accuracy loss, as the network and numeric precision remain fixed. Unlike prior work that optimizes only hardware or only mapping, our approach jointly optimizes both. We show that reconfiguring at carefully chosen points reduces overall inference latency despite reconfiguration costs. On GPT-2, ResNet-18, VGG01, VGG02, and AlexNet, our cluster-based designs reduce latency by 20–43% versus a fixed architecture and outperform the Simba and Eyeriss accelerators on four of five models while matching performance on VGG02.

abstract: Sequential recommendation methods are important in recommender systems, as they capture users’ dynamic interests from their historical behavior sequences. However, most existing methods have two limitations. First, they heavily rely on semantics from only a target user's interaction sequence, despite users and items with limited interactions being prevalent in real-world scenarios. Second, they suffer from popularity bias. Although data augmentation techniques have been proposed to address these issues, they struggle to augment the user with relevant and diverse data, and have limitations in dealing with popularity bias or responding to it excessively. Hence, we propose a new sequential recommendation framework that learns popularity-aware user representations via retrieval-augmentation, called REDS, to improve the quality of recommendations for users with sparse interactions and to mitigate popularity bias by: (i) incorporating embeddings of how often each item occurs in all users’ interactions into a user representation, (ii) augmenting the representation with her/his top- \(k\) similar users’ representations by leveraging the user's supervision signals during training, and (iii) disentangling the user preference into two factors to capture complementary semantics between the target user's and her/his similar users’ interaction sequences. Experiments on three real-world datasets show that REDS outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. The source code is available at https://github.com/JaneHubb/REDS .

abstract: Thanks to advances in the field of computer graphics and natural language processing, it is increasingly possible to create multimedia applications that use a hyper-realistic avatar as the main element of the communication interface with the user. However, major challenges remain, especially when the avatar is required to simulate the appearance and behavior of a real person. This work describes the methodology and tools necessary to create a hyper-realistic avatar that simulates the appearance and behavior of a real person. The methods and tools have been tested by developing a new application that simulates the sports training process. The design of the new application is based on the hypothesis that a digital system that hyper-realistically simulates real training can offer similar benefits to the real one and, therefore, be used to complement real training sessions and thus facilitating the continued performance of the exercise. In this work, a complete sports training simulator has been developed with special emphasis on simulating the coach's real appearance, his way of moving and speaking, as well as a personalized exercise routine generator. Finally, a between-subjects study was conducted comparing sessions led by a real coach versus his hyper-realistic digital twin. Twelve people participated in two 15-minute sessions, one with each type of coach. The analysis was performed using user experience questionnaires and physiological metrics captured through tracking bands during training sessions. The questionnaires indicated that users positively value the system as a complementary tool to their usual training routines. On the other hand, physiological metrics revealed that while users initially exert less effort with the digital avatar, their performance levels, in terms of HRV and temperature, tended to align with those of the in-person sessions halfway through the training. These findings provide valuable insights into the effectiveness and impact of digital avatars compared to real coaches in the context of fitness training.

abstract: Audio-driven 3D facial animation has emerged as a prominent research topic in computer graphics. Existing autoregressive methods are often slow and suffer from error accumulation, whereas non-autoregressive methods often struggle to establish global contextual dependencies. Moreover, current approaches remain insufficient in the cross-modal semantic alignment between audio and facial animation. To address these challenges, we propose a non-autoregressive audio-driven 3D facial animation method with multimodal context enhancement. Our method fully exploits multi-scale facial representations as well as the global contextual information within facial and audio feature sequences, enabling deep cross-modal fusion and precise semantic alignment. Specifically, we develop a global–local encoder built with spiral convolution, which facilitates complementary learning of global basic features and local fine-grained details, thereby improving the quality of facial feature extraction. We further design a multimodal context-enhanced cross-modal modulation module. This module adopts an Adaptive Instance Normalization (AdaIN)-based cross-modal fusion strategy to modulate facial features with audio sequence context in a single step, achieving fast generation without error accumulation. In addition, the module constructs a feature region cross-attention mechanism to capture contextual dependencies within facial features, and leverages globally-aware adaptive channel weighting to model temporal contextual relations of multimodal fused features. These designs enable effective exploitation of global context and substantially improve cross-modal semantic alignment accuracy. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms mainstream baselines in both animation quality and generation efficiency.

abstract: Text-to-video retrieval answers user queries through searches based on concepts and embeddings. However, due to limitations in the size of the concept bank and the amount of training data, answering queries in the wild is not always effective because of the out-of-vocabulary problem. Furthermore, neither concept-based nor embedding-based search can perform reasoning to consolidate search results for complex queries that include logical and spatial constraints. To address these challenges, we leverage large language models (LLMs) to paraphrase queries using text-to-text (T2T), text-to-image (T2I), and image-to-text (I2T) transformations. These transformations rephrase abstract concepts into simpler terms to mitigate the out-of-vocabulary problem. Additionally, complex relationships within a query can be decomposed into simpler sub-queries, improving retrieval performance by effectively fusing the search results of these sub-queries. To mitigate the issue of LLM hallucination, this paper also proposes a novel consistency-based verification strategy to filter out factually incorrect paraphrased queries. Extensive experiments are conducted for ad-hoc video search and known-item search on the TRECVid datasets. We provide empirical insights into how traditionally difficult-to-answer queries can be effectively resolved through query paraphrasing.

abstract: Multi-modal hashing converts high-dimensional features into compact binary codes while preserving semantic similarity, thereby achieving high performance with lower storage and computational costs. However, existing methods generally overly depend on discrete supervisory information, ignoring the ambiguity of labels and intra-class diversity. To address these challenges, we propose a novel S emantic S elf-refinement M ulti-modal H ashing (SSMH), which adaptively learns stable semantic representations through a unified end-to-end semantic learning. First, we dynamically integrate inter- and intra- modal correlations to achieve semantically consistent multi-modal integrated representation. Then, we generate prototype-guided binary codes to explicitly align multi-modal representations with label semantics, thereby strengthening supervision and mitigating the effect of ambiguous labels. Extensive experiments show SSMH outperforms state-of-the-art methods in multi-modal retrieval. The source code can be found at https://github.com/vindahi/SSMH.

abstract: Multimodal aspect based sentiment analysis (MABSA) aims to infer the sentiment polarity toward a specific aspect by jointly leveraging textual and visual evidence. Despite recent progress, existing methods still suffer from three major limitations: they often rely on static shared prompts, have limited access to aspect-relevant external knowledge, and remain vulnerable when multimodal cues are noisy, incomplete, or weakly aligned with the target aspect. To address these issues, we propose RAMP , a unified framework that integrates aspect-aware retrieval, dynamic prompt generation, missing-cue compensation, hierarchical prompt encoding, and deep perturbation optimization. Specifically, RAMP first retrieves semantically relevant multimodal instances from an external memory bank to introduce aspect-aware contextual evidence beyond the current sample. It then converts the retrieved evidence into instance-specific prompts through a context-aware dynamic prompting mechanism, while adaptively compensating for unreliable or incomplete modalities. The generated prompts are further refined by a hierarchical prompt encoder and injected into multiple Transformer layers through deep perturbation, enabling shallow retrieved knowledge and deep semantic guidance to be consistently integrated. Finally, an aspect-guided aggregation module produces the sentiment prediction. Extensive experiments on Twitter-2015, Twitter-2017, and MASAD demonstrate that RAMP consistently outperforms strong baselines in both Accuracy and Macro-F1.

abstract: Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) integrates physical laws into neural network training to solve complex problems governed by differential equations. A critical component in PIML is computing derivatives of models to ensure compliance with the governing equations. A common approach is to use automatic differentiation (AD) methods available in machine learning frameworks such as PyTorch, which is accurate but not always the most efficient approach. An alternative AD method is demonstrated here in the context of physics-regularized genetic programming with symbolic regression (PR-GPSR). This work introduces Hypercomplex-based Automatic Differentiation (HYPAD), which utilizes the Order Truncated Imaginary (OTI) library to efficiently compute second- and fourth-order derivatives in PR-GPSR applications via BINGO, an open-source symbolic regression library. Numerical experiments demonstrate that HYPAD achieves up to a \(123\times\) runtime improvement over PyTorch implementations, with both approaches recovering the correct solutions in the demonstrated PR-GPSR problems. HYPAD evaluates functions by propagating OTI hypercomplex numbers through a command array representation, enabling computation of arbitrary-order derivatives. The approach may also be applicable beyond symbolic regression, motivating further investigation in other PIML and AD applications.

abstract: Precision emulation algorithms, such as the Ozaki schemes, can leverage low-precision matrix multiply–accumulate to approximate the product \(AB\) , where \(A\) and \(B\) are high-precision floating-point matrices, via fixed-point arithmetic. A key difficulty of these approaches is that achieving a target floating-point precision \(p\) requires a fixed-point bit width \(w=p+\star\) , where the required number of extra bits \(\star\) depends strongly on the matrix coefficients. The exponent span capacity (ESC), recently introduced in the literature, is an upper bound \(\overline{e}\geq\star\) . For square matrices of order \(n\) , the ESC can be estimated with \(O(n^{2}k)\) operations, where the parameter \(k\) can be increased to improve the sharpness of \(\overline{e}\) . We show that this bound can be very pessimistic, and that for the estimator to be useful, \(k\) must scale with \(n\) , effectively incurring an \(O(n^{3})\) overhead. Building on a rigorous error analysis, we then derive a new formula for \(\star\) , which corroborates the previously proposed formula up to a few bits. We propose an alternative, sharper bound, which can be computed with \(O(n^{2}k)\) operations, where \(k\) becomes independent of \(n\) . Our numerical experiments demonstrate that the current approach can substantially overestimate \(\star\) in many cases, whilst our new approach is almost perfectly sharp even for moderate values of \(k\) . We present strategies for handling matrices with zero coefficients and give a refined formulation for \(\star\) , in which different fixed-point bit widths are used for \(A\) and \(B\) . Overall, this work provides rigorous theoretical accuracy guarantees for fixed-point emulation and a practical algorithm to inexpensively yet sharply determine the required fixed-point bit width.

abstract: Missing security checks on critical variables are an important class of semantic bugs in the Linux kernel and can lead to severe vulnerabilities. Existing approaches largely rely on static analysis, but heuristic rule-based and statistical approaches may fail to capture the semantic context needed to determine whether a security check is required. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer an opportunity to complement static analysis with semantic reasoning. However, directly applying LLMs to kernel code remains challenging, particularly in identifying critical variables and interpreting security-check semantics. To address these challenges, we present LLMSA-MC, a framework that combines static analysis with LLM-based semantic reasoning for missing-check bug detection. LLMSA-MC incorporates three strategies: (1) Statement Type Classification, which guides LLMs to identify critical variables; (2) Precise Code Context Extraction, which provides relevant code context for semantic reasoning; and (3) Function Label Generation, which annotates function return values with semantic labels. Evaluation on curated intra- and inter-procedural benchmarks shows that LLMSA-MC improves F1-score by up to 39.01 and 33.66 percentage points, respectively, over baseline chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting. When integrated with a representative missing-check bug detection tool, LLMSA-MC reduces candidate reports by 55.38% while confirming 168 missing-check bugs in Linux kernel v4.20-rc5.

abstract: Mobile Crowdsensing (MCS) faces persistent challenges in user participation, data freshness (Age of Information), privacy, and scalability in decentralized environments. We introduce HMOM-MCS , a focused framework deliberately centered on three interdependent pillars: (1) the novel Hybrid Bald Eagle Search–Gazelle Optimizer (BES-GO) that efficiently solves the non-convex, time-dependent, multi-objective incentive problem with sublinear regret \(O(\sqrt {T\log T}) \) under standard online-learning assumptions; (2) a strict mobile-edge-fog-cloud architecture that reduces decision-making latency by 30–40% while enabling real-time incentives; and (3) a participation-centric incentive suite (entry lotteries for newcomers, social referral bonuses, and reputation multipliers) that works synergistically with federated-learning-based user profiling and blockchain settlement. In simulation, and under the behavioral assumptions described in the paper, this design achieves 21–52% higher social welfare, raises the participation rate from below 60% to 85%, attains 98% task completion, lowers information latency by 16–25%, and reduces energy consumption by 20–25% compared to state-of-the-art baselines. On the theory side, we establish incentive compatibility for the VCG core augmented with bid-independent bonuses (with the scope of the remaining incentive terms delimited explicitly), individual rationality, budget feasibility, and sublinear regret under standard online-learning assumptions. Extensive simulations on real-world traces (Rome Taxi, Geolife, Foursquare, CRAWDAD) and ablation studies indicate that, under the simulation settings considered, removing any of the three pillars causes statistically significant performance degradation ( p < 0.001). These results are simulation-based: they characterize behavior under our modeling assumptions rather than measured real-world participation, and human-subject validation in a live testbed remains an essential direction for future work. All code and data are publicly accessible at https://github.com/Ali-Hosseini5422/HMOM-MCS-Simulator.

abstract: Abstract Bloom filter is a widely used classic data structure for approximate membership queries. Learned Bloom filters improve memory efficiency by leveraging machine learning, with the partitioned learned Bloom filter (PLBF) being among the most memory-efficient variants. However, PLBF suffers from high construction cost, with time complexity $$\mathcal {O}(N^3k)$$ O ( N 3 k ) , where N and k are hyperparameters. In this paper, we propose three methods, fast PLBF , fast PLBF++ , and fast PLBF# , that reduce the construction complexity to $$\mathcal {O}(N^2k)$$ O ( N 2 k ) , $$\mathcal {O}(Nk \log N)$$ O ( N k log N ) , and $$\mathcal {O}(Nk \log k)$$ O ( N k log k ) , respectively. Fast PLBF preserves the original PLBF structure and memory efficiency. Although fast PLBF++ and fast PLBF# may have different structures, we theoretically prove they are equivalent to PLBF under ideal data distribution. Furthermore, for non-ideal scenarios, we introduce an instance-specific measure of deviation from the ideal distribution and use it to bound the resulting difference in memory efficiency between PLBF and fast PLBF++. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that, under the default setting ( $$N=1000$$ N = 1000 and $$k=5$$ k = 5 ), fast PLBF, fast PLBF++, and fast PLBF# are up to 58.7, 74.5, and 75.7 times faster to construct than original PLBF, respectively. In an ablation with larger k , which enables the construction of more accurate PLBFs, the speedups reach 235, 865, and 871 times at $$k=50$$ k = 50 . Additionally, fast PLBF maintains the same data structure as PLBF, and fast PLBF++ and fast PLBF# achieve nearly identical memory efficiency.

abstract: Abstract The shortest path counting is an important problem for various applications in road networks, such as traffic analysis, reliability assessment, and navigation services. Existing methods, such as 2-hop labeling schemes, precompute shortest-path distances and counts to enable fast query responses, but they face scalability challenges in large and dynamically changing networks. In this work, we propose an efficient solution, Dynamic Count Labeling (DCL) , for shortest path count queries on dynamic road networks. DCL consists of three key components: a tree hierarchy , a 2-hop count labeling scheme , and a shortcut count graph scheme . The tree hierarchy organizes the network to guide the 2-hop labeling design and ensures efficient query processing by limiting the search space to a small subset of relevant label entries. The shortcut count graph scheme enables efficient construction and dynamic maintenance of the 2-hop labels under edge weight increases and decreases. We further develop dynamic algorithms to update both the shortcut count graph and the 2-hop labels in response to network changes. Additionally, we introduce a parallel version of our algorithms that leverages the label structure for high parallel efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that DCL can compete with existing approaches for static graphs in terms of construction time, index size and query time, while enabling efficient index updates for dynamic graphs, at a fraction of reconstruction costs.

abstract: Maximizing monotone submodular functions under a matroid constraint is a classic algorithmic problem with multiple applications in data mining and machine learning. We study this significant problem in the fully dynamic setting, where elements can be both inserted and deleted in real-time. Our main result is a randomized algorithm that maintains an efficient data structure with an \({\tilde{O}(\frac{{k^{2}}}{{\varepsilon}})}\) amortized update time (in the number of insertions and deletions) and yields a \({(4+O(\varepsilon))}\) -approximate solution with respect to the dynamic optimum, where \(k\) is the rank of the matroid.

abstract: Label-specific features work as an effective supervised feature manipulation strategy to account for distinct discriminative properties of each class label in multi-label classification. Existing approaches implement this strategy in its primal form, i.e., finding the most pertinent features specific to each class label and directly inducing classifiers on these features. Instead of such a straightforward implementation, a dual perspective for label-specific feature learning is investigated in this article. As a dual problem of existing primal one, we consider label-specific discriminative properties by identifying non-informative features for each class label and making the discrimination process immutable to variations of identified features. Accordingly, a perturbation-based approach Dela is presented, which endows classifiers with immutability on simultaneously identified non-informative features by solving a probabilistically relaxed expected risk minimization problem. Furthermore, we touch the realistic issue of label-specific feature learning in a weakly supervised scenario via extending Dela to accommodate to multi-label data with missing labels. Comprehensive experiments show that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art counterparts.

abstract: While language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their performance remains disproportionately skewed towards high-resource languages. This disparity is particularly acute for the 700 million inhabitants of Southeast Asia, where vast linguistic diversity remains under-represented in existing benchmarks, often suffering from limited language coverage or narrow task scopes. To address this, we introduce DeepSEA, a comprehensive benchmark constructed from established datasets through professional human translation into 12 Southeast Asian languages, spanning both high-resource (e.g., Indonesian, Thai, Vietnamese) and low-resource (e.g., Burmese, Khmer, Lao) languages across five distinct tasks: mathematical reasoning, scientific reasoning, question answering, abstractive summarisation, and machine translation. Extensive evaluation of frontier proprietary and openweights models reveals that while frontier models like Gemini-3.7-Flash maintain robustness across resource tiers, smaller models face severe performance degradation on low-resource languages. Crucially, models perform better in reasoning and summarisation when pivoted through English rather than target languages, exposing a critical dependency on English representations, especially for low-resource languages. Beyond these observations, we provide a cross-lingual error analysis and a cross-script tokeniser fertility analysis. We hope these findings shed light on the development of next generation inclusive multilingual models.

abstract: We present PopResume, a population-representative resume dataset for causal fairness auditing of LLM- and VLM-based resume screening systems. Unlike existing benchmarks that rely on manually injected demographic information and outcome-level disparities, PopResume is grounded in population statistics and preserves natural attribute relationships, enabling path-specific effect (PSE)-based fairness evaluation. We decompose the effect of a protected attribute on resume scores into two paths: the business necessity path, mediated by job-relevant qualifications, and the redlining path, mediated by demographic proxies. This distinction allows auditors to separate legally permissible from impermissible sources of disparity. Evaluating four LLMs and four VLMs on PopResume’s 60.8K resumes across five occupations, we identify five representative discrimination patterns that aggregate metrics fail to capture. Our results demonstrate that PSE-based evaluation reveals fairness issues masked by outcome-level measures, underscoring the need for causally-grounded auditing frameworks in AI-assisted hiring.

abstract: Text-labeled graph databases combine symbolic graph structures with rich textual descriptions, enabling expressive representations for real-world data. However, answering queries over such databases remains challenging when queries require both precise logical constraints and flexible semantic text interpretation, especially under information incompleteness. We introduce the task of hybrid query answering (hybrid QA) over incomplete text-labeled graph databases, which requires joint reasoning over both symbolic and textual knowledge under incompleteness. To investigate this problem, we formalize a query language that integrates logical constraints with free-form textual descriptions and construct two new benchmark datasets from biological and e-commerce domains. We propose HybridQE, a hybrid query embedding framework that aligns with our query language via embedding and combining the symbolic and textual constraints in a unified embedding space. Experiments on the proposed benchmarks show that existing methods struggle with this setting, while HybridQE provides consistent improvements across diverse hybrid query types, highlighting both the difficulty of HybridQA and the promise of hybrid query embeddings for reasoning under incompleteness.

abstract: Hate speech detection is inherently subjective: people from different demographic groups perceive the same content very differently. Collecting enough annotations from multiple demographic groups is costly and difficult to scale. Persona-conditioned Large Language Models (models prompted to adopt a specific demographic identity) have been proposed as a way to simulate diverse perspectives at scale. But do they actually reflect how different groups disagree? We evaluate three aspects of human social judgement: (i) whether personas from different groups disagree in human-like ways (inter-group disagreement), (ii) whether they become more sensitive when content targets their own identity (in-group sensitivity), and (iii) whether they can accurately predict how another group would react (vicarious prediction). Our results show that no model consistently captures all three dimensions, and performance is highly model-dependent and does not emerge reliably from minimal identity prompts alone. However, vicarious prompting with Llama 3.1 yields the highest cross-group agreement in most demographic axes and provides the closest overall approximation to human disagreement patterns, indicating that this configuration may provide a more reliable setting for automatic annotation aligned with human judgements.

abstract: News consumption on social media has become ubiquitous, yet how different forms of engagement shape psychosocial outcomes remains unclear. To address this gap, we leveraged a large-scale dataset of ~26M posts and ~45M comments on the Bluesky platform and conducted a quasi-experimental study, matching 81,345 Treated users exposed to News feeds with 83,711 Control users using stratified propensity score analysis. We examined psychosocial wellbeing in terms of affective, behavioral, and cognitive outcomes. Our findings reveal that news engagement produces systematic trade-offs: increased depression, stress, and anxiety, yet decreased loneliness and increased social interaction on the platform. Regression models reveal that News feed bookmarking is associated with greater psychosocial deterioration compared to commenting or quoting, with magnitude differences exceeding tenfold. These per-engagement effects accumulate with repeated exposure, showing significant psychosocial impacts. Our work extends theories of news effects beyond crisis-centric frameworks by demonstrating that routine consumption creates distinct psychological dynamics depending on engagement type, and bears implications for tools and interventions for mitigating the psychosocial costs of news consumption on social media.

abstract: Flowchart-oriented dialogue (FOD) systems aim to guide users through multi-turn decision-making or operational procedures by following a domain-specific flowchart to achieve a task goal. In this work, we formalize flowchart reasoning in FOD as grounding user input to flowchart nodes at each dialogue turn while ensuring node transition is consistent with the correct flowchart path. Despite recent advances of LLMs in task-oriented dialogue systems, adapting them to FOD still faces two limitations: (1) LLMs lack an explicit mechanism to represent and reason over flowchart topology, and (2) they are prone to hallucinations, leading to unfaithful flowchart reasoning. To address these limitations, we propose FloCA, a zero-shot flowchart-oriented conversational agent. FloCA uses an LLM for intent understanding and response generation, while delegating flowchart reasoning to an external tool that performs topology-constrained graph execution, ensuring faithful and logically consistent node transitions across dialogue turns. We further introduce an evaluation framework with an LLM-based user simulator and five new metrics covering reasoning accuracy and interaction efficiency. Extensive experiments on FLODIAL and PFDial datasets highlight the bottlenecks of existing LLM/VLM-based methods and demonstrate the superiority of FloCA.

abstract: The public often attributes human-like qualities to large language models (LLMs), assuming that they "know" certain things. In reality, LLMs encode information retained during training as internal probabilistic knowledge. This study examines existing methods for probing the veracity of that knowledge and identifies three flawed underlying assumptions. To address these flaws, we introduce ‘sAwMIL‘ (Sparse-Aware Multiple-Instance Learning), a multiclass probing framework that combines multiple-instance learning with conformal prediction. ‘sAwMIL‘ leverages LLMs’ internal representations to classify statements as _true_, _false_, or _neither_. We evaluate ‘sAwMIL‘ across 16 open-source LLMs, including default and chat-based variants, using three new curated datasets. Our results show that (1) common probing methods fail to provide a reliable and transferable veracity direction and, in some settings, perform worse than zero-shot prompting; (2) truth and falsehood are not encoded symmetrically; and (3) LLMs encode a third type of signal that is distinct from both true and false.

abstract: Large language models have shown impressive capabilities in code generation, yet they often produce functionally incorrect code. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods have emerged as a promising approach for detecting hallucinations in natural language generation, but their effectiveness for code generation tasks remains underexplored. We systematically evaluate how UQ techniques transfer to code generation across three programming languages, five LLMs, and over 1,700 problems. We find that some token-probability-based methods generalize effectively without modification, while sampling-based methods relying on natural language inference (NLI) fail because NLI models cannot distinguish functionally different code, causing most responses to collapse into a single semantic cluster. To address this, we introduce functional equivalence methods, a family of code-specific methods that replace NLI-based semantic equivalence with an LLM-based functional equivalence assessment, including functional entropy, a code-specific analog of semantic entropy. Functional equivalence methods achieve top AUROC in 11 out of 15 model-benchmark combinations and the best calibration across most settings, consistently outperforming both NLI-based counterparts and all other methods evaluated.

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently exhibit performance biases against regional dialects of low-resource languages. However, frameworks to quantify these disparities remain scarce. We propose a two-phase framework to evaluate dialectal bias, operationalized as comprehension degradation relative to standard Bengali, in LLM question-answering across nine Bengali dialects. First, we translate and gold-label standard Bengali questions into dialectal variants adopting a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline to prepare 4,000 question sets. Since traditional translation quality evaluation metrics fail on unstandardized dialects, we evaluate fidelity using an LLM-as-a-judge, which human correlation confirms outperforms legacy metrics. Second, we benchmark 19 LLMs across these gold-labeled sets, running 68,395 RLAIF evaluations validated through multi-judge agreement and human fallback. Our findings reveal severe performance drops linked to linguistic divergence. For instance, responses to the highly divergent Chittagong dialect score 5.44/10, compared to 7.68/10 for Tangail. Furthermore, increased model scale does not consistently mitigate this bias. We contribute a validated translation quality evaluation method, a rigorous benchmark dataset, and a Critical Bias Sensitivity (CBS) metric for safety-critical applications.

abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) show strong zero-shot performance on tasks such as audio question answering, but still lag behind specialized systems on discriminative tasks such as audio classification. Recent work shows that sparse subsets of attention heads can serve as discriminative feature extractors for few-shot classification, but existing methods weight all selected heads equally. We propose \textbf{C}lass-Conditional Sparse \textbf{A}ttention Vectors for Large Audio-\textbf{L}anguage \textbf{M}odels, a few-shot classifier that learns class-conditional importance weights over attention heads. By treating heads as class-specific experts and aggregating them with reliability-weighted soft voting, CALM allows different classes to rely on different subsets of heads. Across diverse few-shot audio, audiovisual, visual, and spoofing benchmarks, CALM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art uniform-voting baselines, with gains of up to 14.52, 1.53, and 8.35 absolute points on audio, audiovisual, and spoofing tasks, respectively.

abstract: Multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) benchmarks in NLP use number-right scoring (accuracy), but in educational testing, the scoring scheme—the combination of the response mode models follow and the rule for grading responses—is a key design choice that dictates which abilities to reward. We examine how alternatives to number right change what MCQA measures with six education-inspired schemes that assess abilities beyond accuracy: distractor elimination, abstention, confidence calibration, and self-correction. On LLM benchmarks, these schemes: 1) shift rankings of 31 LLMs beyond rephrased number right prompts; 2) better predict the LLMs users prefer in LLM Arena; and 3) reveal distinct model capabilities, like that GPT-5 rarely abstains and readily self-corrects, while weaker open-weight models often abstain and hesitate to eliminate choices. Given the benefits of alternative scoring schemes, we discuss ways to extend them to tasks beyond MCQA.

abstract: Multimodal web agents that process both screenshots and accessibility trees are increasingly deployed to interact with web interfaces, yet their dual-stream architecture opens an underexplored attack surface: an adversary who injects content into the webpage DOM simultaneously corrupts both observation channels with a consistent deceptive narrative. Our vulnerability analysis on MiniWob++ reveals that attacks including a visual component far outperform text-only injections, exposing critical gaps in text-centric VLM safety training. Motivated by this finding, we propose Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training (DMAST), a framework that formalizes the agent-attacker interaction as a two-player zero-sum Markov game and co-trains both players through a three-stage pipeline: (1) imitation learning from a strong teacher model, (2) oracle-guided supervised fine-tuning that uses a novel zero-acknowledgment strategy to instill task-focused reasoning under adversarial noise, and (3) adversarial reinforcement learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) self-play. On out-of-distribution tasks, DMAST nearly halves the attack success rate (41.2% \rightarrow 21.4%) while raising task completion by over 60% relative (6.2% \rightarrow 10.2%). Our approach outperforms established training-based and prompt-based defenses, demonstrating genuine co-evolutionary progress and robust generalization to complex, unseen environments. Code is available at https://github.com/huajianduzhuo-code/DMAST_official.

abstract: The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) has transformed many industries, including healthcare. In practice, hospitals and patients increasingly seek LLM-based systems capable of interpreting personal health records and providing healthcare guidance. However, existing approaches mainly rely on general medical knowledge and often fail to account for individual variability, limiting their ability to provide personalized guidance. To address this, we propose personalized prompt learning (PPL), a framework that learns individualized prompts to guide LLMs in generating personalized healthcare recommendations. PPL constructs initial personalized prompts by leveraging both self-informed patient information and peer-informed signals derived from clinically similar cases. These prompts are then refined using reinforcement learning (RL) to better align the generated responses with physician recommendations written for each patient. PPL operates with hard prompts, enabling seamless integration with proprietary LLMs without modifying the underlying models. We evaluate PPL on real-world obstetrics and gynecology data. The results show that our approach produces more personalized healthcare guidance and wins 97 out of 100 comparisons in expert evaluation, demonstrating its potential for broader healthcare applications. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/CGCL-codes/PPL.

abstract: Persona prompting can steer LLM generation towards a domain-specific tone and pattern. This behavior enables use cases in multi-agent systems where diverse interactions are crucial and human-centered tasks require high-level human alignment. Prior works provide mixed options on their utility: some report performance gains when using expert personas for certain domains and their contribution to data diversity in synthetic data creation, while others find near-zero or negative impact on general utility. To fully leverage the benefits of the LLM persona and avoid its harmfulness, a more comprehensive investigation of the mechanism is crucial. In this work, we study how model optimization, task type, prompt length, and placement can impact expert persona effectiveness across instruction-tuned and reasoning LLMs, and provide insight into conditions under which expert personas fail and succeed. Based on our findings, we developed a pipeline to fully leverage the benefits of an expert persona, named PRISM (Persona Routing via Intent-based Self-Modeling), which self-distills an intent-conditioned expert persona into a gated LoRA adapter through a bootstrapping process that requires no external data, models, or knowledge. PRISM enhances human preference and safety alignment on generative tasks while maintaining accuracy on discriminative tasks across all models, with minimum memory and computing overhead.

abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on clinical text understanding, they struggle with longitudinal prediction tasks such as dementia prognosis, which require reasoning over complex, non-monotonic symptom trajectories across multiple visits. Standard supervised training lacks explicit annotations for symptom evolution, while direct Reinforcement Learning (RL) is hindered by sparse binary rewards. To address this challenge, we introduce Dementia-R1, an RL-based framework for longitudinal dementia prognosis from unstructured clinical notes. Our approach adopts a Cold-Start RL strategy that pre-trains the model to predict verifiable clinical indices extracted from patient histories, enhancing the capability to reason about disease progression before determining the final clinical status. Extensive experiments show that Dementia-R1 achieves the best overall performance on a real-world unstructured cohort, reaching an AUROC of 84.02% and outperforming models up to 10 larger. The framework also generalizes to Parkinson’s disease dementia prediction in an independent hospital cohort, achieving an AUROC of 78.37%. On the ADNI benchmark, our 7B model attains the highest AUROC among all LLM baselines at 83.17%, demonstrating strong longitudinal reasoning over fluctuating cognitive trajectories. Code is available at https://github.com/hangeol/dementiar1.

abstract: Natural language conveys information at varying levels of granularity, from fine-grained references to broad descriptions. While granularity is fundamental to human communication, existing measures mostly capture surface detail or sentence specificity. We introduce Granuscore, a reference-free measure of granularity that leverages structural properties of a hierarchical embedding space. Granuscore reliably recovers hierarchical orderings on the Granola-EQ dataset and captures expected differences in granularity across discourse contexts. Across domains, we further show that Granuscore explains non-linear variation in sentence specificity beyond sentence length. Finally, we apply Granuscore to four question-answering benchmarks and analyze how granularity differs for questions, gold answers, and model outputs across response outcomes. The analysis reveals consistent differences in model behavior and provides a principled lens for characterizing the difficulty of QA datasets. Together, the results position Granuscore as a scalable, broadly applicable tool for analyzing granularity in text.

abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising masked sequences, but standard decoding either fixes the sequence length or relies on ad hoc stopping rules, often leading to unnecessary denoising steps. We recast length selection as a discrete-time survival problem over the end-of-sequence token and propose a plug-in, training-free length predictor that can be added to any existing DLM. Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, survival-guided length decoding speeds up inference by up to 7\times while preserving task accuracy. We further find that predicted lengths vary widely even within the same dataset, making model performance sensitive to the chosen length.

abstract: Large language model (LLM) unlearning has emerged as a crucial post-hoc mechanism for privacy protection and AI safety, yet auditing whether target knowledge is truly erased remains challenging. Existing output-level metrics fail to detect when this knowledge remains recoverable from internal representations. Recent white-box studies reveal such residual knowledge but often rely on auxiliary training or dataset-specific adaptations, leaving no generalizable metric. We close this gap with the Unlearning Depth Score (UDS), a metric that quantifies the mechanistic depth of unlearning via activation patching. UDS first identifies layers that encode the target knowledge using a retain model baseline, then measures how much of it is erased in the unlearned model on a 0-1 scale. In a meta-evaluation across 20 metrics on 150 unlearned models spanning 8 methods, UDS achieves the highest faithfulness and robustness, confirming our causal approach as the most reliable for unlearning evaluation. Case studies further show that UDS uncovers residual knowledge obscured from observational metrics by representational shifts, with erasure depth varying across prompt types. We provide guidelines for integrating UDS into existing benchmarking frameworks and streamlining the evaluation pipeline.

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) incur significant computational and memory costs when processing long prompts, as full self-attention scales quadratically with input length. Token compression aims to address this challenge by reducing the number of tokens representing inputs. However, existing prompt-compression approaches primarily operate in token space and overlook inefficiencies in the latent embedding space. In this paper, we propose K-Token Merging, a latent-space compression framework that merges each contiguous block of token embeddings into a single embedding via a lightweight encoder. The compressed sequence is processed by a LoRA-adapted LLM, while generation remains in the original vocabulary. Experiments on structural reasoning (Textualized Tree), sentiment classification (Amazon Reviews), and code editing (CommitPackFT) show that K-Token Merging lies on the Pareto frontier of performance vs. compression, achieving up to 75% input length reduction with minimal performance degradation.

abstract: Conversational AI systems are increasingly used for personal reflection and emotional disclosure, raising concerns about their effects on vulnerable users. Recent anecdotal reports suggest that prolonged interactions with conversational AI may reinforce delusional thinking—a phenomenon sometimes described as AI Psychosis. However, systematic empirical evidence on this phenomenon remains limited. In this work, we examine how delusion-related language evolves during multi-turn interactions with conversational AI. Using Reddit data, we construct simulated users (SimUsers) from users’ longitudinal posting histories and generate extended conversations with three model families (GPT, LLaMA, and Qwen). We develop DelusionScore, a linguistic measure that quantifies the intensity of delusion-related language across conversational turns. We find that SimUsers derived from users with prior delusion-related discourse (Treatment) exhibit progressively increasing DelusionScore trajectories, while those derived from users without such discourse (Control) remain stable or decline. We further find that this amplification varies across themes, with reality skepticism and compulsive reasoning showing the strongest increases. Finally, conditioning AI responses on the current DelusionScore substantially reduces these trajectories. These findings provide empirical evidence that conversational AI interactions can amplify delusion-related language over extended dialogue and underscore the importance of state-aware safety mechanisms to mitigate such risks.

abstract: The rapid adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) has raised significant environmental concerns. Unlike the one-time cost of training, LLM inference occurs continuously and dominates the AI energy footprint. Yet most sustainability studies report only coarse model-level metrics, treating energy efficiency as an afterthought rather than a primary objective. Addressing the limitation, we propose Component-Level Energy Assessment via Repetitions (CLEAR), to overcome temporal mismatch between microsecond scale component execution and millisecond(ms) scale monitoring of energy sensors. Using CLEAR, we evaluate 15 models spanning four architecture types, keeping component-wise energy variance below 9.5% while capturing over 90% of total energy as individual components. We present the first comprehensive, fine-grained energy analysis of Transformer components across key parameters such as batch size, attention heads, hidden dimension, KV cache, and attention variants. Our findings reveal that Attention consumes significantly more Energy per FLOP as compared to the entire model, indicating that FLOPs alone fail to capture true component-level energy cost. CLEAR enables reliable fine-grained energy measurements and provides a strong formal foundation for predictive modelling of energy consumption.

abstract: Given a query, how can a QA system ask an informative clarifying question to accurately answer it? Open-domain conversational question answering requires not only detecting when a query is ambiguous but also asking clarifying questions that efficiently uncover the latent intent of the user. However, existing approaches either rely on prompt-only clarify-or-answer decisions with limited robustness or distill clarification trajectories without explicitly modeling intent convergence. In this paper, we propose D4CQ (Data-Efficient Diagnosticity based Dynamic Distillation for Clarifying Question), a data-efficient framework for learning diagnostic clarifying questions through dynamic distillation. Our approach distills a structured refinement protocol, prioritizes informative clarifications via diagnosticity-based reweighting, and improves sample efficiency through hindsight relabeling. Empirical results demonstrates that D4CQ consistently outperforms strong baselines, while maintaining comparable interaction budgets. Our code is available at https://github.com/ddddcq/d4cq.

abstract: SQL dialects vary in syntax, types, and functions across database engines. Text-to-SQL benchmarks, however, predominantly support only SQLite. This creates a critical evaluation gap: cross-dialect evaluation reveals weak per-query agreement (Cohen’s ), showing that SQLite performance is an unreliable proxy for other dialects. Yet such evaluation remains prohibitively difficult: existing approaches either require expensive manual query transpilation or rely on tools that often fail on complex SQL. To close this gap, we introduce PolySQL, a novel dual-execution method that eliminates the need for query transpilation by comparing normalized execution results. Notably, our approach achieves higher evaluation fidelity than query transpilation with 100% query coverage. PolySQL comprises three datasets, enabling the first large-scale cross-dialect study. Our study reveals a 10.1% average accuracy drop from SQLite to other dialects and identifies a significant dialect difficulty hierarchy. We find this degradation stems from logical rather than syntactic errors (61% vs. 8%). We release our framework code and leaderboard to enable rigorous dialect-robust evaluation.Code, Results and Environments are shared in https://github.com/IBM/polysql

abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) offer order-agnostic generation that can explore many possible decoding trajectories. However, current decoding methods commit to a single trajectory, limiting exploration in trajectory space. We introduce Order-Token Search to explore this space through jointly searching over generation order and token values. Its core is a likelihood estimator that scores denoising actions, enabling stable pruning and efficient exploration of diverse trajectories. Across mathematical reasoning and coding benchmarks, Order-Token Search consistently outperforms baselines on GSM8K, MATH500, Countdown, and HumanEval (3.1%, 3.8%, 7.9%, and 6.8% absolute over backbone), reaching accuracy comparable to diffu-GRPO post-training. Our work establishes joint search as a key component for advancing decoding in DLMs.

abstract: Human-like agents must express stable dispositions while adapting to roles, relationships, and norms. We present PsyAgent, a schema-first framework that operationalizes the trait–context interface by coupling a Big Five trait prior with explicit social-structural conditioning. PsyAgent comprises (i) Individual Structure (IS), a machine-usable trait-grounded profile, and (ii) Multi-Scenario Contexting (MSC), a curated library of role–relationship–norm frames spanning eight everyday arenas. At inference, fixed structured prompts couple the active MSC frame with the IS profile, encouraging behavior that is stable yet context-sensitive. To demonstrate learnability beyond prompt engineering, we use IS×MSC to synthesize supervision and fine-tune compact backbones with PEFT (SFT and optional DPO). Under a controlled psychometric-style evaluation protocol in percentile space, PsyAgent improves trait-faithfulness and multi-turn persona consistency, and is competitive with several larger general-purpose instruction-tuned baselines under matched decoding and scoring controls. We further triangulate the automatic protocol with external benchmarks and a small blinded human study. Overall, PsyAgent provides a precise and data-efficient approach to personality-grounded, norm-aware agents.

abstract: Healthcare prediction using electronic health records (EHRs) is a cornerstone of modern clinical decision support. Conventional machine learning (ML) models achieve strong predictive performance but rarely provide knowledge-grounded, human-readable explanations. Large language models (LLMs) incorporated with medical knowledge graphs (KGs) offer advanced reasoning and explainability with encoded clinical facts, yet existing approaches typically perform monolithic reasoning over entire patient records, mixing task-irrelevant context and obscuring disease-specific attribution. To bridge these gaps, we propose CRU-Reason, a novel framework that integrates ML models, medical KGs, and LLMs through Clinical Rationale Units (CRUs) for knowledge-grounded and interpretable healthcare prediction. CRU is a localized structure that explicitly captures clinically meaningful communities among EHR concepts, thereby enabling LLMs to perform disease-centered, fine-grained reasoning. Experiments on two public clinical datasets demonstrate that CRU-Reason improves over the strongest evaluated EHR-prediction baselines by an average of +9.4% across drug recommendation and diagnosis prediction, while exhibiting improved rationale quality and cross-dataset robustness.

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various domains, yet they struggle with causal reasoning tasks. We introduce PACKaGE (Paragraph-level Annotated Causal Knowledge and Graph–tExt), a causal benchmark dataset that pairs paragraph-level texts with explicit causal graphs. Unlike prior sentence-level resources, our benchmark dataset (i) operates at paragraph level to capture various and interdependent causal pathways; (ii) offers multimodal annotations including full graphs and contextualized relations; and (iii) maps extended passages to comprehensive graphs. We detail a four-stage construction pipeline: collecting causality-labeled and fact-centric texts, inducing graphs from span-tagged pairs, condensing nodes, and recomposing path-aligned narratives. Overall, the paired evaluation highlights a persistent discrepancy between linguistic competence and causal understanding in LLMs, pointing to the need for further development.

abstract: Modern information retrieval increasingly employs both embedding and generative models to handle complex queries. However, current serving systems suffer from low throughput and poor GPU utilization because they execute these models in isolation. Coarse-grained partitioning, such as dedicating GPUs to specific tasks, fails to adapt to dynamic workloads and creates computational “bubbles”. To address these, we present Orthrus, a serving system that performs heterogeneous batching within a single GPU kernel. The primary challenge lies in unifying embedding and generation workloads with conflicting computational patterns while optimizing batch composition for high performance. Orthrus addresses these challenges by employing incremental computing to match compute patterns and by adjusting batch composition in a workload-aware manner. Evaluation on four A100 GPUs shows that Orthrus achieves 1.28×–4.52× higher throughput and up to 52.0% lower latency than various deployment scenarios based on homogeneous batching, including those built on vLLM. We release our code at [https://github.com/illinoisdata/Orthrus](https://github.com/illinoisdata/Orthrus)

abstract: Spexis is a multi-GPU LLM inference framework that improves the efficiency of pipeline and tensor parallelism through speculative parallelism. Rather than using speculative decoding only to accelerate token generation, Spexis runs speculation in parallel with normal execution, introducing a new parallelism axis without increasing KV-cache memory usage. This improves memory efficiency and helps mitigate the bottlenecks of multi-GPU inference.Spexis further uses lookahead scheduling to predict speculation quality and future memory pressure, allowing it to reduce wasted speculation, KV-cache eviction, and recomputation. Built on top of vLLM, Spexis largely improves serving performance across a range of GPU configurations, achieving speedups of up to 34% over a baseline that uses the optimal combination of pipeline and tensor parallelism. Spexis’s source code is publicly available at https://github.com/mlsys-seo/spexis.

abstract: Estimating the Arabic Level of Dialectness (ALDi) is a continuous regression task that quantifies how much a sentence diverges from Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). While auxiliary classification is often used to support regression, its effectiveness depends critically on how the auxiliary task is designed. We conduct a systematic study of auxiliary classification for ALDi estimation, showing that naive auxiliary supervision can degrade regression performance under skewed target distributions. We identify two key factors that determine when auxiliary tasks become beneficial: the granularity of discretization and the choice of loss function. Specifically, 7-bin discretization combined with focal loss substantially improves performance. Our approach achieves an RMSE of 0.1275 on the NADI 2024 blind test set, outperforming previous systems by over 9%, and the same design transfers to English toxicity regression. Detailed error analysis reveals how auxiliary classification reshapes model behavior across the Arabic dialect spectrum. We release our code and model predictions to facilitate future research

abstract: Multilingual machine translation models must adapt to the grammatical structure of the target language, yet how structural information shapes decoder computation remains unclear. Using the eigenvalue spectra of per-(layer, head) attention Gram matrices instead of raw attention weights, we show that cross-attention geometry in NLLB-200 is organized around the target language: these spectral features carry a strong, distributed signal about target-language word order (SVO vs. SOV) when English is the source, with near-perfect decodability across cross-validation. The signal is not concentrated in a small subset of heads, but is broadly distributed across layers and heads—yet it degrades sharply at every level of aggregation when English is the target. This asymmetry suggests that cross-attention geometry reflects the demands of target-side generation rather than source-side structure. Leave-one-language-out evaluation confirms that the signal generalizes to unseen languages, ruling out language identity as a confound.

title: Cross-Attention Eigenvalues Know the Word Order in Multilingual Machine Translation

abstract: Translated versions of English-origin benchmarks such as MMLU are widely used to evaluate large language models in non-English languages, yet it remains unclear whether they measure the same constructs as natively created benchmarks. We frame this as a *proxy validity* question and compare DeepL-translated MMLU proxies against six native benchmarks in seven pairings across five Nordic and Baltic languages, evaluating 29 models on each pairing. Beyond ranking agreement, we test *incremental* proxy validity: does the translated score add predictive value for native performance after controlling for model size and language proficiency? Proxy validity varies substantially across benchmark pairings. Applying the same robustness criteria to all seven pairings, we find four robust effects, two marginal effects, and one null result. The strongest evidence occurs for curriculum-overlap benchmarks such as Skolprov (\Delta R^2=.128, 95% CI [.038,.253]), whereas translated MMLU provides no significant incremental value for Sweden-specific factual knowledge in SwedishFacts (p=.242). Because SwedishFacts is also the only open-ended benchmark, we cannot fully separate the effects of local content and response format. Overall, the results indicate a clear pattern: translated benchmarks provide a better proxy when their source content overlaps with the native evaluation target, while locally anchored knowledge is less reliably captured.

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently produce confident yet factually incorrect responses when user inputs contain misleading premises, a phenomenon we attribute to fact perturbations in the input. Existing approaches to hallucination mitigation typically assume reliable user inputs, overlooking how such factual errors can actively mislead model reasoning. To address this vulnerability, we propose DEDUCE, a three-stage framework that transforms LLMs from passive responders into proactive error correctors. DEDUCE operates in three stages: (1) detect errors through fine-grained fact extraction and verification; (2) devise correction strategies via multi perspective deliberation; and (3) correct misconceptions while delivering reliable answers. We also present MisFactQA, a dataset containing factual errors of varying degrees, and propose new metrics for evaluating model robustness. Experiments on TruthfulQA, FalseQA, and our MisFactQA benchmark demonstrate that DEDUCE significantly improves both accuracy and error correction capability. Consistent gains across Qwen, LLaMA, and Gemma families confirm its effectiveness and scalability.

title: From Passive Response to Proactive Correction: Enhancing LLM Robustness Against Input Fact Perturbations

abstract: While factual correctness and task-performance have received much attention by Large Language Model (LLM) research, the fundamental question of how human-like generated texts are on a linguistic level has been underexplored. From a corpus-linguistic perspective, language production is inherently context-dependent. Distinct communicative contexts give rise to differences in frequencies and co-occurrence patterns of linguistic features that shape registers of language use. A text failing to adhere to these patterns can be correct content-wise, but still may not appear natural to human readers. In this work, we propose a context-aware evaluation framework in which human-likeness is measured as a two-sample problem between the linguistic feature distribution of a human reference corpus for a given register and a corresponding LLM-generated corpus. We implement this framework using the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) measure and the 67 lexico-grammatical features introduced by Biber, which are commonly applied in corpus linguistics.In our experiments, we compare seven instruction-tuned, open-source models and look at  five English-language datasets spanning distinct registers. While across all tested setups, LLMs deviate from the human baseline, which models are closest to human language depends on the register and is not dictated by model size.

abstract: Document-Level Relation Extraction (DocRE) relies heavily on costly manually annotated datasets, while large distant supervision resources such as DocRED distant remain underexploited due to noise. We show that a critical yet overlooked source of noise lies in structural inconsistencies within relational triples, including violations of ontology constraints and logical contradictions.We introduce an ontology-driven framework to quantify and enforce structural consistency in DocRE datasets. Our analysis reveals substantial structural noise in DocRED distant and demonstrates that such inconsistencies propagate to model predictions. Enforcing structural well-formedness during training significantly reduces logical contradictions and consistently improves generalization performance. These findings establish structural consistency as a missing axis of supervision in DocRE and highlight structural regularization as an effective strategy for leveraging distant data at scale.

abstract: LLMs have shown promise in legal NLP, but generating legal reasoning that is factually grounded, faithful to precedent, and consistent with judicial analysis remains difficult. Retrieval-augmented generation is often used to improve grounding, yet standard legal RAG faces two limitations: retrieved materials are hard to synthesize, and retrieval is driven by surface similarity rather than the latent legal issues and factual considerations that govern the analysis. We address these limitations with SCALE (Structured Case-law-guided Anticipatory Legal reasoning), a framework for precedent-grounded legal reasoning. SCALE converts article-specific Case Law Guides into an Issue–Factor Hierarchy, identifies the issues and factors implicated by a case, retrieves the linked guide passages, and generates the final legal analysis. Across Llama-3.1 and Qwen3 models, expert evaluation shows that SCALE consistently outperforms prompt-only and retrieval-based baselines, with the largest gains in legal issue identification and precedent use. These gains are especially strong for smaller models, suggesting that explicit legal structure can compensate for weaker implicit reasoning capacity. We also compare expert assessment with an LLM-as-a-Judge framework and find only weak-to-moderate agreement, underscoring the limits of automated evaluation for high-stakes legal reasoning.

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of reasoning tasks, yet their understanding of joint and conditional probability distributions remains largely unexplored. In this work, we present a comprehensive evaluation of LLMs’ ability to reason about discrete joint and conditional probability distributions involving multiple random variables. Given observations drawn from a distribution, we evaluate models on three carefully designed tasks—mode identification, maximum likelihood estimation, and sample generation—which together capture fundamental skills required for probabilistic reasoning. Our study reveals both capabilities and limitations of current LLMs. In sample generation task, some models produce empirical distributions that closely match the target distribution despite exhibiting limited sample independence. We further observe that model performance is highly sensitive to representation: replacing explicit frequency information with raw samples leads to large accuracy drops, and even minor changes to outcome labels can further degrade performance. Together, these findings provide new insights into how LLMs reason about discrete joint and conditional probability distributions and highlight their strengths and limitations in certain probabilistic reasoning settings.

abstract: With the increasing size of large language models, layer pruning has gained increased attention as a hardware-friendly approach for model compression. However, existing layer pruning methods struggle to simultaneously address key practical deployment challenges, including performance degradation, high training costs, and limited acceleration. To overcome these limitations, we propose E^3-Pruner, a task-Effective, training-Economical and inference-Efficient layer pruning framework. E^3-Pruner introduces two key innovations: (1) a differentiable mask optimization method using a Gumbel-TopK sampler, enabling efficient and precise pruning mask search; and (2) an entropy-aware adaptive knowledge distillation strategy that enhances task performance. Extensive experiments over diverse model architectures and benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our method over state-of-the-art approaches. Notably, E^3-Pruner achieves 96% accuracy, a mere 0.8% drop from the original model (96.8%) on MATH-500 when pruning 25% layers of Qwen3-32B, outperforming existing SOTA (95%), with a 1.33\times inference speedup by consuming merely 0.5B tokens (0.5% of the post-training data volume).
